quests.instruction: Tap the beat on each stressed syllable as you read it aloud (final stress: -ee, -eer, -ique).
quests.hint: 'trainee', 'engineer' and 'technique' all carry stress on the last syllable: train-EE, en-gi-NEER, tech-NIQUE.
quests.explanation: Words ending in -ee, -eer and -ique are stressed on the ending itself, so the last syllable is long and clear. Earlier syllables are short and weak.
quests.textToSpeak: The trainee asked the engineer to explain the technique.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would talk about a restaurant team.
quests.hint: 'Chinese', 'Japanese' and 'Vietnamese' all end with the stressed syllable -ese: Chi-NESE, Jap-a-NESE, Viet-na-MESE.
quests.explanation: Nationality words ending in -ese carry the main stress on the ending. Before a noun, the stress can move earlier: 'a CHInese restaurant'.
quests.textToSpeak: The chefs are Chinese, Japanese and Vietnamese.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a shopping story.
quests.hint: 'antique', 'boutique' and 'unique' all end with the stressed syllable -ique, said [iːk].
quests.explanation: The ending -ique is pronounced [iːk] and carries the stress. Say the first syllable quickly and lean into the last.
quests.textToSpeak: We bought an antique chair at a boutique that sells unique gifts.

quests.instruction: Tap the beat on each stressed syllable as you read it aloud (stress shifts in a word family).
quests.hint: The stress moves: PHO-to-graph, pho-TOG-ra-pher, pho-to-GRAPH-ic.
quests.explanation: When you add a suffix, the stress often moves. 'photograph' stresses the first syllable, 'photographer' the second, and 'photographic' the third. Vowels change with the stress.
quests.textToSpeak: This photograph is amazing; the photographer must have real photographic talent.
quests.targetPhoneme: stress shifts in a word family
commonMistakes: Stressing the same syllable in all three words
Keeping [oʊ] in the first syllable of 'photographer'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a news comment Watch the stress shifts: economy, economist, economic.
quests.hint: 'economy' is e-CON-o-my, 'economist' is e-CON-o-mist, and 'economic' is e-co-NOM-ic.
quests.explanation: 'economy' and 'economist' share the same stress; the suffix -ic pulls it forward to the syllable before -ic. Learn the pair, then the odd one out.
quests.textToSpeak: The economy is weak, and every economist agrees the economic outlook is poor.
commonMistakes: Stressing 'economic' on the same syllable as 'economy'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a casual opinion.
quests.hint: 'politics' is POL-i-tics, 'politician' is pol-i-TI-cian, and 'political' is po-LIT-i-cal.
quests.explanation: Each suffix moves the stress: -ician stresses the syllable before it, and -ical does the same. Notice how the first vowel is full in 'politics' but weak in the others.
quests.textToSpeak: I'm not into politics, but that politician knows the political situation.
commonMistakes: Saying the first vowel of 'political' as a full [ɒ]

quests.instruction: Tap the beat on each stressed syllable as you read it aloud (reduced syllables).
quests.hint: 'comfortable', 'chocolate' and 'vegetable' lose a syllable in speech: COMF-ter-ble, CHOC-lit, VEG-ta-ble.
quests.explanation: Native speakers skip weak middle vowels: 'chocolate' has two beats, 'vegetable' three, and 'comfortable' three. Say the stressed beat clearly and squash the rest.
quests.textToSpeak: The place is comfortable, and it serves chocolate cake and vegetable soup.
commonMistakes: Saying 'chocolate' as 'choc-o-late' with three full beats

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a recommendation.
quests.hint: 'favourite', 'business', 'average' and 'reasonable' lose weak syllables: FAV-rite, BIZ-ness, AV-rage, REA-zna-ble.
quests.explanation: In these words, a middle vowel is dropped or reduced to almost nothing. Say the words as two or three quick beats, not by spelling.
quests.textToSpeak: My favourite shop is a family business, and the average price is reasonable.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a reflective comment.
quests.hint: 'generally' (GEN-ral-ly), 'different' (DIF-rent) and 'ordinary' (OR-dn-ary) each lose a weak syllable.
quests.explanation: In natural speech, the middle vowels in these words vanish or shrink. 'experience' keeps its stress on the second syllable.
quests.textToSpeak: Generally, it's a different experience every time, and nothing feels ordinary.

quests.instruction: Tap the beat on each stressed syllable as you read it aloud (stress in workplace nouns).
quests.hint: 'accountant' is ac-COUNT-ant, 'consultant' is con-SUL-tant, 'quarterly' is QUAR-ter-ly, and 'budget' is BUD-get.
quests.explanation: Professional nouns ending in -ant take stress on the syllable before it. The last syllable is weak, so 'accountant' ends on [ənt], not [ænt].
quests.textToSpeak: The accountant asked the consultant to review the quarterly budget.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a workplace update Watch the stress in workplace vocabulary.
quests.hint: 'supervisor' (SU-per-vi-sor), 'appointment' (a-POINT-ment), 'agenda' (a-GEN-da) and 'interview' (IN-ter-view).
quests.explanation: Find the stressed beat in each word: SU in 'supervisor', POINT in 'appointment', GEN in 'agenda' and IN in 'interview'. The rest stays weak.
quests.textToSpeak: The supervisor booked an appointment to discuss the agenda for the interview.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would describe a colleague.
quests.hint: 'colleague' is COL-league, 'entrepreneur' is en-tre-pre-NEUR, 'negotiates' is ne-GO-ti-ates, and 'strategy' is STRAT-e-gy.
quests.explanation: 'entrepreneur' ends with the stressed syllable, like -eer words. 'negotiates' puts the stress on 'go' and 'strategy' on 'strat'.
quests.textToSpeak: My colleague is an entrepreneur; she negotiates deals and develops the strategy.
commonMistakes: Saying 'negotiates' with stress on the first syllable

quests.instruction: Tap the beat on each stressed syllable as you read it aloud (stress in academic vocabulary).
quests.hint: 'hypothesis' is hy-POTH-e-sis, 'evidence' is EV-i-dence, and 'literature' is LIT-er-a-ture.
quests.explanation: Longer academic words keep one main stress and weak syllables around it. 'literature' is often said in three beats: LIT-ra-chur.
quests.textToSpeak: The hypothesis is based on evidence from the literature.
commonMistakes: Saying 'literature' as 'lit-er-a-ture' with four equal beats

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a research summary.
quests.hint: 'significant' is sig-NIF-i-cant, 'difference' is DIF-rence, and 'categories' is CAT-e-gor-ies.
quests.explanation: The stressed syllable in 'significant' is 'nif', and the last three are weak. 'difference' is usually said in two beats.
quests.textToSpeak: The study shows a significant difference between the two categories.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a comment in a seminar.
quests.hint: 'phenomenon' is phe-NOM-e-non, 'analyse' is AN-a-lyse, and 'methodology' is meth-o-DOL-o-gy.
quests.explanation: The main stress is on the syllable marked: NOM, AN and DOL. Note that the verb 'analyse' stresses the first syllable, unlike 'analysis'.
quests.textToSpeak: This phenomenon is hard to analyse, so the methodology needs revision.

quests.instruction: Tap the beat on each stressed syllable as you read it aloud (-teen vs -ty stress).
quests.hint: 'thirteen' stresses the last syllable (thir-TEEN); 'thirty' stresses the first (THIR-ty).
quests.explanation: In -teen numbers, the ending is stressed and the vowel is long. In -ty numbers, the first syllable is stressed and the ending is short. Before a noun, -teen may shift: 'THIRteen rooms'.
quests.textToSpeak: We booked thirteen rooms, not thirty.
commonMistakes: Stressing the same syllable in both words
Adding a [n] to the end of 'thirty'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a correction to a price.
quests.hint: 'fifteen' is fif-TEEN, and 'fifty' is FIF-ty.
quests.explanation: The contrast is in stress and vowel length. Lengthen [iː] in the -teen number and shorten the ending of the -ty number.
quests.textToSpeak: The tickets were fifteen euros each, not fifty.
commonMistakes: Giving 'fifty' the stress on the second syllable
Making the ending of 'fifty' as long as [iː]

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a joke about your age.
quests.hint: 'nineteen' is nine-TEEN, and 'ninety' is NINE-ty.
quests.explanation: Both start with the same syllable, so the difference is the stress and the last vowel. Lengthen the last syllable in 'nineteen', and keep 'ninety' quick.
quests.textToSpeak: I'm nineteen, but people say I look ninety.
commonMistakes: Saying 'ninety' with a long final vowel

quests.instruction: Tap the beat on each stressed syllable as you read it aloud (stress in initialisms).
quests.hint: In initialisms said letter by letter, the last letter is stressed: PDF is pee-dee-EFF, HR is aitch-AR, and CEO is see-ee-OH.
quests.explanation: Say each letter clearly, and give the last one the most stress and the highest pitch. Don't run the letters together.
quests.textToSpeak: Send the PDF to HR, and copy the CEO.
commonMistakes: Running the letters together as one word

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as instructions at a help desk.
quests.hint: 'USB', 'ID' and 'IT' are all said letter by letter, with stress on the last letter.
quests.explanation: The article changes with the sound: 'an ID' and 'an IT' take 'an' because they start with vowel sounds, while 'a USB' takes 'a' because it starts with [j].
quests.textToSpeak: You'll need a USB cable and an ID card for the IT desk.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as an online-banking tip.
quests.hint: 'FAQ' and 'SMS' are letter names, while 'PIN' is pronounced as one word.
quests.explanation: Some abbreviations are said letter by letter, and others as words. 'PIN' rhymes with 'tin'. 'FAQ' can be either letters or [fæk].
quests.textToSpeak: The FAQ says your PIN is sent by SMS.

quests.instruction: Tap the beat on each stressed syllable as you read it aloud (phrasal verb stress).
quests.hint: In 'turn down' and 'work out', the second word (the particle) gets the main stress: turn DOWN, work OUT.
quests.explanation: In phrasal verbs, both words are stressed, but the particle is stronger and higher in pitch. Say the verb clearly, then peak on the particle.
quests.textToSpeak: Could you turn down the music? I can't work out the answer.
quests.phoneticHint: 'turn down' is [ˌtɜːrn ˈdaʊn] and 'work out' is [ˌwɜːrk ˈaʊt].
commonMistakes: Giving the verb and the particle the same weight
Pausing between the verb and the particle

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a travel instruction.
quests.hint: As a verb, 'check in' stresses the particle (check IN); as a noun, 'check-in' stresses the first part (CHECK-in).
quests.explanation: The same words change stress with their job: verb phrase = particle stress, noun compound = first-part stress.
quests.textToSpeak: We have to check in early; the check-in desk closes at ten.
quests.targetPhoneme: verb vs noun stress: check in
quests.phoneticHint: the verb is [ˌtʃek ˈɪn] and the noun is [ˈtʃek ɪn].
commonMistakes: Using the same stress for both

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a problem-solving story.
quests.hint: With a pronoun, the particle is the stressed word: looked it UP. 'figure out' also peaks on OUT.
quests.explanation: When a short pronoun like 'it' comes between the verb and the particle, keep 'it' weak and move the peak to the particle.
quests.textToSpeak: I couldn't figure out the problem, so I looked it up in the manual.
quests.phoneticHint: 'figure out' is [ˌfɪgjər ˈaʊt] and 'looked it up' is [ˈlʊkt ɪt ˈʌp].

quests.instruction: Tap the beat on each stressed syllable as you read it aloud (stress in country and nationality words).
quests.hint: 'Japan' is ja-PAN and 'Japanese' is Jap-a-NESE. The stress is on the last syllable in both, but 'Japanese' is longer.
quests.explanation: Country and nationality words can shift stress, and with the suffix -ese the stress is on the ending. Learn each pair separately.
quests.textToSpeak: My Japanese friend is planning a trip to Japan.
quests.targetPhoneme: stress in country and nationality words

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a sports comment.
quests.hint: 'Canadian' is ca-NA-di-an, 'Australian' is aus-TRA-lian, and 'Italian' is i-TAL-ian.
quests.explanation: Nationality words ending in -ian stress the syllable before the ending. Compare 'Canada' (CAN-a-da) and 'Italy' (IT-a-ly), where the stress is earlier.
quests.textToSpeak: The Canadian team beat the Australian and Italian teams.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as you would introduce yourself and your family.
quests.hint: 'Portuguese' is por-tu-GUESE, 'Vietnamese' is viet-na-MESE, and 'Argentina' is ar-gen-TI-na.
quests.explanation: The -ese words stress the ending, and 'Argentina' stresses the syllable before -a. All the earlier syllables stay quick and weak.
quests.textToSpeak: I'm Portuguese, my wife is Vietnamese, and we're moving to Argentina.
quests.targetPhoneme: stress in nationality and country words

quests.instruction: Tap the beat on each stressed syllable as you read it aloud (mixed stress review).
quests.hint: Find the main stress: JOUR-na-list, re-COR-ded, IN-ter-view, pol-i-TI-cian, e-co-NOM-ic, POL-i-cy.
quests.explanation: This sentence mixes four rules: verb stress on the second syllable, first-syllable stress in 'interview' and 'journalist', -ician stress, and -ic stress. Apply each in turn.
quests.textToSpeak: The journalist recorded an interview with a politician about economic policy.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a news report.
quests.hint: 'volunteers' (vol-un-TEERS), 'thirty' (THIR-ty), 'donations' (do-NA-tions), and 'community' (com-MU-ni-ty).
quests.explanation: Combine -eer, -ty, -tion and -ity stress rules. Say the stressed beat first, then squash the weak syllables around it.
quests.textToSpeak: Yesterday, the volunteers packed thirty boxes of donations at the community centre.
commonMistakes: Saying 'thirty' with stress on the second syllable

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a customer-service complaint.
quests.hint: 'unfortunately' (un-FOR-tu-nate-ly), 'delivery' (de-LIV-er-y), 'customer' (CUS-to-mer), 'requested' (re-QUEST-ed), 'refund' (REE-fund), 'compensation' (com-pen-SA-tion).
quests.explanation: Six words, six stress patterns. Rehearse each stressed beat: FOR, LIV, CUS, QUEST, REE and SA. Keep the other syllables short.
quests.textToSpeak: Unfortunately, the delivery was late, so the customer requested a refund and asked for compensation.
quests.phoneticHint: 'unfortunately' is [ʌnˈfɔːrtʃənətli], 'delivery' is [dɪˈlɪvəri], 'requested' is [rɪˈkwestɪd], 'refund' (noun) is [ˈriːfʌnd], and 'compensation' is [ˌkɒmpənˈseɪʃən].
